chunks: Muhammad ibn Ya'qub narrated from al-Husayn ibn Muhammad, from Mu'alla ibn Muhammad, from al-Hasan ibn Ali al-Washsha', from Aban ibn Uthman, from Abd al-Rahman ibn Abi Abdillah, from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) who said:

I asked him about a man who swears to another man regarding food, telling him to eat, but he does not eat; is there expiation for him in that, and what is the oath in which expiation becomes obligatory? He said: 'The expiation is for the one who swears regarding an item that he will not sell it or not buy it, then it becomes apparent to him [that one of the options is better], so he expiates for his oath. And if he swears regarding something, and doing it is better than leaving it, let him do what is better and there is no expiation for him. That is from the 'steps of Satan'.'
ai.seo_question: What is the difference between an oath requiring expiation and one that does not in Shia jurisprudence?
ai.summary: Shaykh al-Tusi records this narration from Imam al-Sadiq (AS) to clarify the distinction between oaths of abstention, which require expiation upon breaking, and oaths of commission, where performing the better of the two options exempts one from expiation. The Imam links the concept of breaking oaths to the Quranic phrase 'steps of Satan,' emphasizing that frivolous or broken vows are a spiritual detriment. This ruling highlights the Shia jurisprudential principle of choosing the superior action (khayr) when an oath is made regarding a permissible matter.
